'''Douglas Richard Flutie''' (born October 23, 1962) is an American former [[Gridiron football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played professionally for 21 seasons. Flutie played 12 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), eight seasons in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL), and one season in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Boston College Eagles football|Boston College Eagles]], winning the [[Heisman Trophy]] in 1984 amid a season that saw him throw a [[Hail Flutie|game-winning touchdown pass]] in the final seconds of a ranked matchup against the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://massmoments.org/moment.cfm?mid=337|title=Doug Flutie Throws 'Hail Mary' Pass|website=massmoments.org|date=November 23, 2006 |access-date=July 8, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Sullivan |first=Mark |title=Famous Flutie pass now in its own class |url=https://web.archive.http://www.bc.edu/bc_org/rvp/pubaf/chronicle/v10/n1/pass.html |access-date=June 11, 2022 |work=Boston College Chronicle |date=November 1, 2001 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141012114229/http://www.bc.edu/bc_org/rvp/pubaf/chronicle/v10/n1/pass.html |archive-date=October 12, 2014 |location=Chestnut Hill}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://msn.foxsports.com/nfl/story/Ten-Best-Damn-unforgettable-sports-moments |title=FOX Sports on MSN – NFL – Ten Best Damn unforgettable sports moments |publisher=Msn.foxsports.com |access-date=January 9, 2014 |url-status = dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140516222405/http://msn.foxsports.com/nfl/story/Ten-Best-Damn-unforgettable-sports-moments |archive-date=May 16, 2014 }}</ref> Flutie chose to begin his professional career with the USFL's [[New Jersey Generals]]; his unavailability to NFL teams resulted in him being selected 285th overall by the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in the 11th round of the [[1985 NFL draft]], the lowest drafting of a Heisman winner.<ref>{{cite web |last=Goldberg |first=Dave |title=Flutie's Salary May Be Big, but the USFL Is Thinking Small |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-02-10-sp-3502-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |access-date=October 20, 2021 |date=February 10, 1985}}</ref> After the USFL folded, Flutie spent his first four NFL seasons with the [[Chicago Bears]] and [[New England Patriots]].

Flutie left the NFL in 1990 for the CFL, where he became regarded as one of the league's greatest players.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/feature/?fid=10867 |title=#1 - DOUG FLUTIE |access-date=April 27, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070427071859/http://www.tsn.ca/cfl/feature/?fid=10867 |archive-date=April 27, 2007 |url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Shire |first=Taylor |date=February 29, 2012 |title=Canadian Football League Power Rankings: The 7 Best Players in CFL History |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1086293-canadian-football-league-power-rankings-the-7-best-players-in-cfl-history |access-date=March 19, 2024 |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Filoso | first=Santino | title=The top 10 quarterbacks in CFL history | website=3DownNation | date=February 6, 2017 | url=https://3downnation.com/2017/02/06/top-10-qbs-cfl-history/ | access-date=April 26, 2025}}</ref> As a member of the [[BC Lions]], [[Calgary Stampeders]], and [[Toronto Argonauts]], he was named the [[CFL's Most Outstanding Player Award|CFL's Most Outstanding Player]] a record six times and won three [[Grey Cup]]s. In all three of his championship victories, two with the Argonauts and one with the Stampeders, he was named [[Grey Cup Most Valuable Player|Grey Cup MVP]].

After his CFL success, Flutie returned to the NFL in 1998 with the [[Buffalo Bills]], earning [[Pro Bowl]] and [[National Football League Comeback Player of the Year Award|NFL Comeback Player of the Year]] honors for leading Buffalo to the playoffs. Flutie again helped the Bills obtain a playoff berth the following season, but was controversially benched in their [[Music City Miracle|subsequent Wild Card defeat]]. He would be the last quarterback to lead the Bills to the playoffs for the next 17 years. Flutie held his last starting role with the [[San Diego Chargers]] in 2001 and spent his final season in 2005 as a backup for the Patriots. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2007 and the [[Canadian Football Hall of Fame]] in 2008. Flutie was also inducted to [[Canada's Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2007, becoming the first non-Canadian inductee.

'''Herbert Dorsey Levens''' (born May 21, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily for the [[Green Bay Packers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]] and later the [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets]]. Levens was selected by Green Bay in the fifth round of the [[1994 NFL draft]]. He helped the Packers win the [[Vince Lombardi Trophy]] in [[Super Bowl XXXI]] against the [[New England Patriots]].

In his career, Levens also played for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and [[New York Giants]]. While playing for the Packers, he rushed for 1,000 or more yards twice and was selected to the [[1998 Pro Bowl|Pro Bowl]] after the [[1997 Green Bay Packers season|1997 season]].

[[Nevada Wolfpack football|Nevada]] | teams = * [[Miami Dolphins]] ([[1978 NFL season|1978]]–[[1987 NFL season|1987]]) | highlights = * [[AP NFL Defensive Player of the Year|NFL Defensive Player of the Year]] (1983) * First-team [[All-Pro]] ([[1983 All-Pro Team|1983]]) * [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1984 Pro Bowl|1983]]) * [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll]] | statlabel1 = [[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] | statvalue1 = 64.5 | statlabel2 = [[Fumble|Fumble recoveries]] | statvalue2 = 6 | pfr = BettDo00 }} '''Douglas Lloyd Betters''' (born June 11, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for the [[Miami Dolphins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1978 to 1987. After graduating from [[Arlington High School (Illinois)|Arlington High School]] in [[Arlington Heights, Illinois]], Betters played college [[Division I (NCAA)|Division I]] football for the [[Montana Grizzlies football|Montana Grizzlies]] from 1974 to 1976, then transferred to play for the [[Nevada Wolf Pack football|Nevada Wolf Pack]] in 1977. The next year, he was a sixth round [[NFL Draft|draft pick]] for the Dolphins. Betters was a part of Miami's "Killer B's" defense, and went to [[Super Bowl XVII]] and [[Super Bowl XIX|XIX]]. In 1983, Betters recorded 16 [[quarterback sack|sack]]s in 16 games and won the [[NFL Defensive Player of the Year Award]], and was named to the [[American Football Conference|AFC]] [[Pro Bowl]] team.{{cite web | title=1983 NFL Pro Bowlers | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1983/probowl.htm | work=Pro Football Reference | access-date=July 10, 2017}} In '83 and '84, Betters was named the Miami Dolphins "Outstanding Defensive Lineman." Betters played 146 NFL games and made {{frac|64|1|2}} career sacks ({{frac|46|1|2}} official, post–1981). He was named by the fans to the Dolphins' Silver Anniversary Team in 1991 and the Golden Anniversary Team in 2016. Betters was an assistant coach for the University of Montana Grizzlies in 1995 and 1996. Doug guided fly fishing on the Flathead River in Montana for Glacier Wilderness Guides and class 4 whitewater on the Lochsa River in Idaho for Lewis and Clark Trail Adventures after his retirement from the NFL. In 1998, Betters suffered a [[spinal cord]] injury while [[skiing]] at [[The Big Mountain|Big Mountain]] in [[Whitefish, Montana]].{{cite magazine | title=A Better Man, the Better Way | url=http://mmqb.si.com/mmqb/2015/12/23/nfl-doug-betters-miami-dolphins-1983-defensive-player-of-year-paralyzed-skiing-accident-montana | magazine=Sports Illustrated | access-date=July 10, 2017}} Betters founded the Doug Betters Winter Classic Organization in 1985, which provides money for children in need of medical care. Betters is involved with numerous other charitable organizations, including the [[Special Olympics]] and [[United Way of America|United Way]]. In 2002, he received the [[Big Brothers Big Sisters of America|Big Brothers/Big Sisters]] of Montana Award. As of 2014 he resides in Whitefish. On December 14, 2008, Betters was inducted into the [[The Miami Dolphin Honor Roll|Miami Dolphins Ring of Honor]] during a ceremony at Dolphin Stadium.

'''Douglas Gordon Brown''' (born September 29, 1974) is a Canadian former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL).  He played [[college football]] at [[Simon Fraser University]].  Brown won the [[CFL's Most Outstanding Canadian Award]] in 2001. He played for the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] from 2001 until his retirement in 2011, competing in three [[Grey Cup]]s:  [[89th Grey Cup|2001]], [[95th Grey Cup|2007]], and [[99th Grey Cup|2011]].  He was a CFL All-Star eight times.

'''Douglas Shirl Barnett Jr. ''' (born April 12, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a defensive end and long snapper in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]], the [[Los Angeles Rams]], and the [[Atlanta Falcons]].

Barnett was selected by the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in the fifth round (118th overall) of the [[1982 NFL draft]]. He appeared in 58 regular-season games over five NFL seasons (1982–1987), including stints with the Rams, [[Washington Redskins]], and [[Atlanta Falcons]]. During his professional career, he recorded one fumble recovery. <ref>{{cite news |title=Skins sign Barnett |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/potomac-news-skins-sign-barnett/175767741/ |access-date=2 July 2025 |work=[[Potomac News]] |agency=[[The Associated Press]] |date=8 October 1985 |page=B7 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref name="HoF" />  

With the Rams, Barnett snapped for punts and kicks in 1982 and 1983, before being hurt in the 1983 playoffs, an injury that kept him out of the 1984 season. He was also a backup defensive end his first two NFL seasons for he likes of Jack Youngblood and Reggie Doss. He was released in August 1985 and trying to come back from his knee injuries. <ref>{{cite news |title=Skins sign Barnett |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/potomac-news-skins-sign-barnett/175767741/ |access-date=2 July 2025 |work=[[Potomac News]] |agency=[[The Associated Press]] |date=8 October 1985 |page=B7 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref name="HoF" /> 

The following year Barnett was signed by Washington and he played two games for them. He was released the following August and didn't play in the NFL in 1986. In 1987 he signed with th Atlanta Falcons, playing ten games for them.

He played [[college football]] for the [[Azusa Pacific Cougars football|Azusa Pacific Cougars]]. Barnett was selected as the first Azusa Pacific player to earn a spot on the [[National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics|NAIA]] All-American first team in 1981. He holds the school record for quarterback sacks in a single game (8) and in a single season (19). <ref>{{cite news |last1=LePage |first1=David |title=Tackle 'Elated' Over Call From Rams |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-tackle-elated-ov/175768323/ |access-date=2 July 2025 |work=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=29 April 1982 |page=9 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |department=Part IX: San Gabriel Valley}}</ref>

He was inducted into the [[Azusa Pacific]] Hall of Fame in 1992. He was a nine-time All-American in college football and track and field, and a member of both the Azusa and NAIA Halls of Fame competing on the track team from 1978 through 1982. 

In track and field, Barnett was a standout thrower, winning the NAIA national championship in the [[hammer throw]] in both 1981 and 1982. He also claimed the NAIA indoor [[shot put]] title in 1981. Overall, he garnered nine All-American honors across football and track and field during his collegiate tenure.<ref name="HoF">{{cite web |title=Doug Barnett (1992) - Hall of Fame |url=https://athletics.apu.edu/honors/hall-of-fame/doug-barnett/7 |website=Azusa Pacific University Athletics |access-date=2 July 2025 |language=en}}</ref> After his retirement from professional football, he was the varsity football head coach for [[Bakersfield Christian High School]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schultz |first1=Dan |title=Bakersfield Christian scrapes past Cavaliers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/tulare-advance-register-bakersfield-chri/175768670/ |access-date=2 July 2025 |work=[[Tulare Advance-Register]] |agency=[[Visalia Times-Delta|Visalia Times-Delta News Service]] |date=20 September 2008 |location=Tulare, California |page=4B |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

'''Benjamin Douglas Hudson''' (born September 11, 1964)<ref name="Hudson"/> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He graduated from [[Gulf Breeze High School]] and played [[college football]] for the [[Nicholls State Colonels football|Nicholls State Colonels]]
<ref>{{cite web | title=Doug Hudson | url=http://www.geauxcolonels.com/documents/2012/8/13/2012%20Nicholls%20Football%20Media%20Guide.pdf?id=446 | publisher= geauxcolonels.com | access-date=2008-09-24}}</ref>

Hudson is best known for a one-play gaffe resulting in a [[Safety (American football score)|safety]].<ref name="Cordill">{{cite web | title=Chiefs' historical strike-out celebrates 21st anniversary | work=University News | url=http://media.www.unews.com/media/storage/paper274/news/2008/09/22/Sports/Daves.Place.Chiefs.Historical.StrikeOut.Celebrates.21st.Anniversary-3444629.shtml | date=2008-09-22 | last=Cordill | first=David | access-date=2008-09-24 }}{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> It is the only recorded statistic of his career.<ref name="Hudson">{{cite web | title=Doug Hudson | work=Pro Football Reference | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HudsDo20.htm | access-date=2008-09-24}}</ref>

Hudson, selected by Kansas City in the [[1987 NFL draft]], was the last quarterback drafted by the Chiefs to [[Starting lineup|start]] a game until [[Brodie Croyle]] started in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-01 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Huard out">{{cite web | agency=Associated Press | title=Huard out, Croyle in as Chiefs' starting quarterback | work=ESPN| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3107200 | date=2007-11-12 | access-date=2008-09-24}}</ref> Hudson was one of five quarterbacks to start a game for the Chiefs in 1987 following a [[Strike action|strike]] by the [[National Football League Players Association]].<ref name="History 80s">{{cite web | title=Kansas City Chiefs History–1980's | work=Kansas City Chiefs official website| url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/history/80s/ | access-date=2008-09-24 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080501122552/http://www.kcchiefs.com/history/80s/ <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 2008-05-01}}</ref>

Hudson played only five minutes in his only game against the [[Denver Broncos]], and he threw one pass for an [[Incomplete pass|incompletion]].<ref name="drought">{{cite web|title=Gretz: The end of the QB/Draft drought |last=Gretz |first=Bob |url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2007/11/14/gretz_the_end_of_the_qbdraft_drought/ |date=2007-11-14 |access-date=2008-09-24 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071217055347/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2007/11/14/gretz_the_end_of_the_qbdraft_drought/ |archive-date=December 17, 2007 }}</ref> He was [[Tackle (football move)|tackled]] by the Broncos' [[Jim Ryan (linebacker)|Jim Ryan]],<ref name="October 18, 1987"/> and [[fumble]]d the hand-off in the [[end zone]]. Hudson recovered the ball but it was recorded as a [[safety (American football score)|safety]].<ref name="drought"/><ref name="October 18, 1987">{{cite web | title=Denver Broncos at Kansas City Chiefs – October 18, 1987 | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198710180kan.htm | access-date=2008-09-24}}</ref> The next time the Chiefs had the ball, Hudson was replaced at quarterback by [[Matt Stevens (quarterback)|Matt Stevens]] and Hudson never played another game in the league.<ref name="drought"/>
